lines.text: Zoom into your phone screen, closer, closer. It's millions of tiny lights. And each one is a sandwich.
Every pixel is made of three smaller lights: red, green, and blue. Mix them, and you get every color you see.
A typical phone screen has around three million pixels. That's about nine million tiny lights.
In an OLED screen, each light is a thin layer of special organic material. Push electricity through it, and it glows by itself.
No backlight needed. So to show black, a pixel just switches off completely. That's why OLED black is truly black.
Now the sandwich. At the bottom, a layer of tiny transistors. Each one controls one light, deciding how bright it shines.
Above that, the glowing organic layers, thinner than a human hair, sealed tight, because air and water would ruin them.
Then a touch layer that feels your finger, a filter to cut glare, and on top, the cover glass.
On foldable phones, the base isn't glass at all. It's a flexible plastic, so the whole screen can bend.
And the newest screens can slow down to just one refresh a second when nothing moves, to save battery.
So next time you scan an Orbi Transfer QR code off a friend's screen, remember, it's millions of tiny lights. Scan it, and their file is yours.
